proposals.impact: convert 3 stalled quiz sessions into starts
proposals.observation: Three sessions hit the quiz intro page in 48 hours. Zero started. The furthest-step distribution shows all three stopped at intro_load, meaning the page rendered but nobody pressed go. No traffic source variation — all direct. This is not a discovery problem. The intro screen is the drop point.
proposals.proposal: The quiz intro screen is asking people to commit before they know what they are committing to. The fix is a one-sentence reframe directly above the start button: tell the person what they will find out, not what they are about to do. Replace the current button-adjacent framing with copy that names the actual output (their specific money script) and sets a realistic time expectation. One sentence. One file. No layout change required.
proposals.current_text: Take the quiz to find out your money personality.
proposals.new_text: In five minutes you'll see which money script has been running your decisions, written up for you in plain English.

proposals.observation: The Money Vigilance automation has a 63.64% open rate on 11 sends, the highest of the three active sequences. Money Avoidance is at 50% and Money Worship sits at 37.5%. Vigilance readers are clearly engaged, but there is no data showing click-through, which suggests the email body may be generating interest without directing it anywhere concrete. A sequence with that open rate and no recorded downstream action is leaving warm readers at a dead end.
proposals.proposal: Add a single, specific call-to-action sentence at the close of the Money Vigilance email body, pointing readers to the blog post or a booking link. The sentence needs to earn its place by connecting directly to what a vigilance-type reader actually does: they research thoroughly, delay acting, and trust evidence over enthusiasm. The CTA should reflect that psychology rather than pushing urgency. One sentence added to the closing paragraph of the automation copy file.
proposals.current_text: If any of this feels familiar, that's worth sitting with.
proposals.new_text: If any of this feels familiar, the next honest step is reading how other careful earners have made sense of the same pattern — Joel's notes are here: [blog link].

proposals.observation: The blog post published today ("Why do I keep dropping every hobby, goal, and budget the moment the novelty wears off?") has no recorded internal links in the commit diff and lands in a queue that is down to two posts. The post topic — novelty-seeking and follow-through — maps precisely onto the ICP's core self-description and would be a natural on-ramp to the quiz, where they would receive a named money script. Without a link, a reader who finishes the post has nowhere to go.
proposals.proposal: Add a closing paragraph to the novelty-drop blog post that connects the behavioural pattern in the article to the quiz, using language grounded in the post's own argument. The paragraph should not summarise the article (readers just read it) and should not feel like a generic plug. It should feel like a natural next thought Joel would say in a session after a client described that exact pattern.
proposals.new_text: That pattern of dropping things, including budgets, often has a money script underneath it that is doing real work. If you want to see which one is operating for you, the five-minute quiz at [quiz link] will show you, in plain English, what it is.
